title: A hymn in Dhanasri
hook: Dhanasri holds Guru Nanak's sky aarti, and near its end, the Bhagats' aartis

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Dhanasri, a raga of true wealth that opens with a frightened soul, and your line was true wealth. What did you give that didn't come from a wallet? Today closes the week. Day one thousand eighty-five.

Aarti is a way of honoring what is dear by waving light before it: a tray of small flames, lifted and circled slowly. Back in year two, you met Guru Nanak's hymn that takes the tray and throws it wide: the sky is the platter, the sun and moon are its lamps, the stars are pearls. Today, notice where it lives: Raga Dhanasri. And if you keep turning the pages of Dhanasri to the end, you find more aartis waiting, sung by the Bhagats. Today: a hymn in Dhanasri, and the conversation its aartis have with each other.
screen: `A TRAY OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.` → `MORE AARTIS AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Start with Guru Nanak's hymn, gagan mai thaal, the sky as the platter. The wind is incense, the forests are flowers, and the whole universe is already performing the aarti. Nobody needs to light anything. Now turn toward the end of the raga, where the Bhagats' hymns sit. Ravidas, remembered by tradition as a leather worker, sings in paraphrase: your Name is my aarti and my cleansing bath. Then he takes the tray apart piece by piece. Your Name is the lamp, the oil, the wick. Without the Name, everything else is show. Sain, remembered as a barber, prepares incense, lamp and ghee for an aarti, and says he would give himself for the Lord. And Dhanna, remembered as a farmer, opens with the word aarta, which some readers hear as an aarti and others as the cry of a humble petitioner. In paraphrase, he asks the Lord plainly for what a household needs: lentils and flour and ghee, shoes and clothes, a milk cow, a good horse, a good wife. His offering is a list from a farmhouse kitchen. Put them together. Guru Nanak lifts the aarti up to the sky. Ravidas brings it inward, into the Name. Sain holds the lamp with devotion. Dhanna sets it down on the kitchen table. The Granth keeps all four voices in the same raga. Look back over this week and the same pattern runs through it: longing at night in Bihagra, wedding and mourning in Vadhans, steady faith and calm in Sorath, true wealth in Dhanasri. Each raga holds more than one kind of heart. Today's line: the sky's aarti.
screen: `THE SKY IS THE PLATTER.` · `RAVIDAS: YOUR NAME IS MY AARTI.` · `SAIN'S LAMP, DHANNA'S KITCHEN.` · `ONE RAGA, MANY KINDS OF HEART.` · then, large: `THE SKY'S AARTI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: an aarti without a tray. If you can, play a Dhanasri shabad first, gagan mai thaal if you find it. Then sit. Let your attention move outward, the way Guru Nanak's hymn does: the light in the room, the air moving, whatever sky is above the roof. Then bring it inward, the way Ravidas does, to one word resting in the breath. Then set it down, the way Dhanna does, on one plain thing your household needs today, and let yourself want it honestly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru at each step. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Dhanasri. Guru Nanak's aarti with the sky as the platter, answered near the raga's end by the aartis of Ravidas, Sain and Dhanna. Today's word.
Your line: the sky's aarti. Step outside once today, or to a window, and look up long enough to notice the platter and its lamps. Day one thousand eighty-five. A week of ragas, done.

howItsDone: Guru Nanak's gagan mai thaal is part of the Kirtan Sohila said at night and is sung in kirtan; the Bhagats' aarti hymns from the end of Dhanasri are also sung, and some Sikh congregations sing a sequence of these aartis together.

original.note: aarti, honoring what is dear by waving light before it; Dhanasri holds several.

trapdoor: what you thought: aarti means waving a tray of lamps.
what it means: in Dhanasri, the whole sky performs it, and the Bhagats make it the Name, a lamp of devotion, and a farmer's honest list.
what a scholar hears: one raga holds a sequence of aartis, Guru Nanak's near the start and Ravidas's, Sain's and Dhanna's near the end, each answering the others.

notes: Year two (days 427–429) already opened gagan mai thaal word by word and told the Puri story; this day avoids retelling them and takes the angle of the Dhanasri section as a sequence of aartis.

All four hymns are paraphrased. Please confirm the Angs (663, 694, 695, 695) and that Ravidas's lamp/oil/wick imagery, Sain's incense, lamp and ghee, and Dhanna's list (lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, clothes, a milk cow, a good horse, a good wife) are fairly summarized.
Dhanna's hymn opens 'Gopal tera aarta'; readers interpret aarta in more than one way (a humble petitioner; an aarti). The script calls his hymn an aarti; please confirm that is acceptable.
The trades of Ravidas, Sain and Dhanna are given as 'remembered by tradition'.

howItsDone: 'some Sikh congregations sing a sequence of these aartis together' refers to the aarti-arta sung in some gurdwaras; practice varies and some Sikh bodies discourage ritual lamp-waving. Please confirm the wording.
